work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: Self-assembly emerges from cells sharing a common model of organismal form
statement: In simulations based on variational free-energy minimization (active inference), cells that share a common genetically and epigenetically specified model of the organism's form self-assemble into that form, offering a proof of principle that self-assembly can be an emergent property of such cells.
quote: Here, we offer a proof of principle that self-assembly is an emergent property of cells that share a common (genetic and epigenetic) model of organismal form.
scope: Active-inference simulation of eight cells forming a head–body–tail morphology

work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: Genome parametrizes a generative model; epigenesis inverts it
statement: Under the free-energy account of morphogenesis, genetic codes can be interpreted as parametrizing a generative model that predicts the signals each cell would sense in the target morphology, and epigenetic processes (signalling-dependent transcription) as the inversion of that model.
quote: This novel perspective on the coordination of migration and differentiation of cells suggests an interpretation of genetic codes as parametrizing a generative model—predicting the signals sensed by cells in the target morphology—and epigenetic processes as the subsequent inversion of that model.
scope: Morphogenesis in multicellular organisms

work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: Morphogenesis requires each cell to model its place in the target form
statement: Friston, Levin, Sengupta and Pezzulo propose that morphogenetic self-organization requires each cell to have an implicit model of its place in the final morphology, with self-assembly being cells moving to sample the local signals that model predicts (minimizing variational free energy).
quote: In this paper, we pursue the notion that morphogenetic self-organization requires each cell to have an implicit model of its place in the final morphology [21]—and that self-assembly is the process of moving to sample local signals that are predicted by that model.
scope: Cells during embryogenesis and regeneration

work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: Free energy is minimized only when every cell occupies a unique inferred place
statement: In the active-inference model of morphogenesis, where identical pluripotent cells share one generative model, the minimum of variational free energy is reached only when every cell is at a unique location and has correctly inferred its place, so free-energy minimization guarantees convergence to the target form.
quote: This is guaranteed because the minimum of variational free energy is obtained when each cell is in a unique location and has correctly inferred its place.
scope: Active-inference model of morphogenesis with cells sharing a generative model

work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: Simulated cells resolve fate ambiguity using context set by other ambiguous cells
statement: In the active-inference simulation, identical undifferentiated cells starting at one location migrate rapidly to their target locations and then differentiate (around the eighth time step) into head, body and tail types as ensemble free energy falls, showing cells can resolve ambiguity about their fate even when it depends on context set by other equally ambiguous cells.
quote: These results are compelling in the sense that they show cells can resolve ambiguity about their fate, even when that resolution depends upon the context established by other (equally ambiguous) cells.
scope: Active-inference simulation of eight cells forming a head–body–tail morphology

work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: Bisected simulated embryos regenerate the full target form
statement: When the partially differentiated simulated embryo is cut in two and each half's cells are replicated, the cells undergo slight dedifferentiation and then each half regenerates the complete head–body–tail target morphology, illustrating pluripotency and recovery from drastic interventions in the active-inference model.
quote: This example illustrates the pluripotential nature of the cells and the ability of self-assembly to recover from fairly drastic interventions.
scope: Active-inference morphogenesis simulation (analogous to planarian or regulative embryo bisection)

work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: Altering signal sensitivity without changing the model predicts specific birth defects
statement: In the active-inference morphogenesis model, changing cells' sensitivity to extracellular, exogenous or intracellular signals without changing the generative model produces specific dysmorphogenesis, e.g. reducing sensitivity to the head-expressed signal shrinks the head, and doubling sensitivity to intracellular signals causes failed migration, differentiation and atrophy; these are predictions for pharmacological manipulation of intercellular signalling.
quote: More selective interventions produce a dysmorphogenesis of various segments of the target morphology: reducing sensitivity to the second chemotactic signal—that is expressed by head cells—reduces the size of the head.
scope: Active-inference morphogenesis simulation; proposed for real embryos under signalling perturbation

work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: Neural and bioelectric patterning networks may share dynamics
statement: Because non-neuronal cells use many of the same ion-channel and electrical-synapse mechanisms as neurons for pattern formation and repair, significant commonalities may exist between the dynamics of neural networks and of bioelectric signalling networks that control shape, so neural modelling tools such as dynamic causal modelling may apply to morphogenesis data.
quote: This suggests the possibility that significant commonalities may exist between the dynamics of neural networks and of bioelectric signalling networks that control shape determination [20,21,83].
scope: Non-neural tissues with bioelectric signalling during development and regeneration

work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: An exogenous gradient makes self-assembly more robust for larger ensembles
statement: In the active-inference morphogenesis simulations, an exogenous concentration gradient is not necessary but yields a more robust solution for larger ensembles (more than four clones) and fixes the orientation of the target morphology relative to an external frame of reference.
quote: This is not a necessary component of the scheme; however, our simulations suggest that it underwrites a more robust solution for larger ensembles (with more than four clones).
scope: Active-inference morphogenesis simulation

work: Knowing one's place: a free-energy approach to pattern regulation
label: Epigenetic active inference is indispensable for patterning beyond genetic encoding
statement: Although aspects of the target morphology are genetically encoded in the parameters of cells' generative models, epigenetic processes (active inference) are indispensable for patterning, consistent with the regenerative target morphology of planaria being permanently alterable (to two heads) by a brief modification of electric synapses.
quote: It may be worth concluding that although aspects of the target morphology are genetically encoded (in the parameters of the generative models); epigenetic processes (active inference) are indispensable for patterning.
scope: Morphogenesis and regeneration, e.g. planarian regeneration

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Brief gap-junction blockade makes G. dorotocephala regenerate other species' head shapes
statement: In decapitated Girardia dorotocephala fragments, a transient perturbation of cell-to-cell physiological connectivity with the gap junction blocker octanol can lead to regenerated heads whose shapes stochastically match those of other planarian species (Schmidtea mediterranea, Dugesia japonica, Polycelis felina).
quote: after decapitation in G. dorotocephala, a transient perturbation of physiological connectivity among cells (using the gap junction blocker octanol) can result in regenerated heads with quite different shapes, stochastically matching other known species of planaria (S. mediterranea, D. japonica, and P. felina)
scope: Regenerating pre-tail fragments of genetically wild-type Girardia dorotocephala treated with octanol (123 µM, 3 days)

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Octanol-induced head shapes are morphometrically closer to the species they resemble
statement: By geometric morphometrics (Procrustes distances), the octanol-induced head shapes of G. dorotocephala regenerates are closer to the wild-type head shapes of the species they resemble than to the wild-type G. dorotocephala head shape.
quote: Comparisons of the Procrustes distances between shape groups (Figure 2A, Table 1) showed that the experimentally derived morphologies were closer in shape to the wild-type morphologies they resembled than the wild-type Girardia dorotocephala head morphology.
scope: Landmark-based head shapes of octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates and wild-type G. dorotocephala, D. japonica, S. mediterranea and P. felina

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Induced head shapes are stochastic, with frequencies tracking evolutionary distance
statement: Under identical octanol treatment, G. dorotocephala regenerates take one of several discrete head shapes, and the frequencies of the shapes are unequal and correlate roughly with the evolutionary distance (from rRNA phylogeny) between G. dorotocephala and the species each shape resembles, with shapes of closer relatives (S. mediterranea, D. japonica) more frequent than that of the more distant P. felina.
quote: We conclude that not only are phenotypic outcomes from physiological network perturbation stochastic (as the same treatment leads to one of several discrete shapes among individuals), but the frequencies are not equal and correlate roughly with evolutionary distance between the worm species these heads resemble.
scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates; four planarian species placed on an rRNA-based tree

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Gap-junction-perturbed worms also acquire the brain shape of the species they resemble
statement: G. dorotocephala regenerates whose heads resemble another species after octanol treatment also have brain morphologies (length/width ratio, by anti-synapsin staining) resembling the brains of wild-type worms of that species.
quote: Strikingly, we found that pseudo worms possessed brain morphologies that look like the brain morphologies of wild-type worms whose head shapes they resembled (Figure 4D–F) (ANOVA, p < 0.001).
scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates compared with wild-type G. dorotocephala, D. japonica and S. mediterranea

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Perturbed worms adopt the anterior stem-cell distribution of the species they resemble
statement: In octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates, the transformation toward another species' head shape extends to the species-characteristic distribution of neoblasts (mitotic stem cells) in the anterior body, and the authors conclude that the patterning processes disrupted by gap junction perturbation also organize the distribution of mitotically active cells.
quote: We conclude that the transformation of G. dorotocephala worms to resemble other species also extends to the species-specific, characteristic internal distribution of their stem cells, and that the patterning processes that are disrupted after GJC perturbation are also responsible for organizing the distribution of mitotically active cells.
scope: Phospho-histone H3-positive neoblasts in the anterior sixth of octanol-treated G. dorotocephala and wild-type G. dorotocephala, D. japonica and S. mediterranea

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Octanol-treated worms show more isopotential regions, which return to normal by 30 days
statement: Ten days after transient octanol exposure, regenerated G. dorotocephala show more distinct isopotential (membrane-voltage) regions by DiBAC dye imaging than controls, and the number of isopotential regions returns to the wild-type level after 30 days of morphological remodeling.
quote: We detected an increased number of isopotential regions in the pseudo worms compared to the states of control worms; interestingly, the numbers of isopotential regions return to those of a wild-type state after 30 days of morphological remodeling (Figure 6I).
scope: Whole-body DiBAC4(3) voltage-dye images of octanol-treated and control G. dorotocephala at 10 and 30 days

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Induced head shapes remodel back toward G. dorotocephala after regeneration ends
statement: The other-species head shapes induced in G. dorotocephala by octanol are not permanent: between days 10 and 30, after regeneration is complete and without further injury, the heads are remodeled to more closely resemble wild-type G. dorotocephala.
quote: We found that the induced morphologies were remodeled, long after regenerative processes had ended, to produce morphologies that bore closer resemblance to wild-type G. dorotocephala.
scope: Octanol-induced pseudo-species G. dorotocephala photographed daily from day 10 to day 30

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Head remodeling passes from S. mediterranea-like to D. japonica-like to normal shape
statement: In canonical variate shape space, the D. japonica head morphology lies between those of G. dorotocephala and S. mediterranea, and octanol-induced S. mediterranea-like G. dorotocephala heads remodel by moving from S. mediterranea-like to D. japonica-like to G. dorotocephala morphology.
quote: DJ morphology lies between GD and SM morphologies in this space, and we observe remodeling that moves from SM morphology to DJ morphology to GD morphology.
scope: Remodeling octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates, days 10–30

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Agent-based model of migrating, signaling cells reproduces the observed head shapes
statement: In an agent-based model of planarian head regeneration in which static somatic cells emit a chemical signal and migratory cells (neoblasts or their progeny) are repelled by it, deactivating different subsets of signaling cells (representing octanol gap-junction blockade) reproduces the four observed head shapes, so a small set of gap-junction-regulated cell behaviors such as migration and cell-cell signaling can quantitatively explain the observed morphologies.
quote: We conclude that a small set of cell-level behaviors, such as migration and cell-cell signaling that are known to be regulated by GJC and thus are perturbed by octanol exposure [35,39,49,98,101,102], can quantitatively explain the morphologies we observed in planaria.
scope: The authors' two-cell-type agent-based model of the planarian head with an elastic boundary

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Coherent discrete head shapes show the octanol effect is instructive rather than toxic
statement: The octanol-induced head-shape change in G. dorotocephala is instructive rather than a toxic or housekeeping defect, because it yields one of several coherent, ecologically valid morphologies rather than regeneration failure or disorganized growth, with no intermediate morphologies observed.
quote: The head morphology alteration effect was instructive, and not merely one of toxicity or a house-keeping defect, because the outcome was not merely disruption of regenerative ability or a generalized mis-patterning (e.g., tumor or other disorganized growth), but rather resulted in one of several coherent (and ecologically-valid) morphologies.
scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Hexanol, which does not block gap junctions, does not alter head shape
statement: In G. dorotocephala, the same 3-day exposure to hexanol, a closely related alcohol that does not efficiently block gap junction channels, does not produce altered head morphologies, consistent with the head-shape change depending on octanol's gap-junction-blocking activity rather than a generalized effect of long-chain alcohols.
quote: The same 3-day treatment with the closely related alcohol, hexanol (6-OH), which does not efficiently block gap junction channels, and subsequent regeneration in water for 7 days, did not produce altered morphologies, consistent with the importance of the GJ-blocking activity of octanol, and not some other generalized effect of long-chain alcohols.
scope: Regenerating G. dorotocephala fragments treated with hexanol versus octanol

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Bioelectric networks derive distinct morphologies from one genome
statement: Physiological bioelectric networks are a previously unrecognized input by which distinct morphologies, including those of other species, can be derived from the same genome, as shown by gap-junction perturbation in G. dorotocephala.
quote: Here, we identify a novel physiological input into the process by which distinct morphologies can be derived from the same genome: physiological bioelectric networks.
scope: Planarian head regeneration (G. dorotocephala), proposed as a general input to morphogenesis

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Brief gap-junction blockade persistently alters bioelectric state after drug washout
statement: In G. dorotocephala, the long-lasting alteration of bioelectric patterning after brief octanol exposure is not caused by residual octanol (which leaves tissues within 24 h) but is initiated by octanol's disruption of gap junction communication, which alters bioelectric network topology and results in a persistent perturbation of bioelectric state.
quote: Although these long-lasting alterations in bioelectrical patterning are not directly caused by octanol remaining within the body of the worm (since 8-OH is known to depart planarian tissues within 24 h [20]), they are initiated by the octanol-mediated disruption of GJC, which alters bioelectric network topology, and results in persistent perturbation of bioelectric state.
scope: G. dorotocephala somatic tissues after transient octanol exposure

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Partial, variable gap-junction blockade is consistent with stochastic head-shape outcomes
statement: The variability and overall magnitude of the bioelectric effect imply that octanol only partially shuts down gap junction communication in each G. dorotocephala (affecting some percentage of gap junctions per animal), which the authors consider consistent with the stochasticity of the head-shape phenotype.
quote: The variability and overall magnitude of the effect imply that the result of 8-OH exposure is only partially effective in shutting down GJC (affecting some percentage of GJs in any animal); this is consistent with the stochasticity of the morphological phenotype (Figure 3).
scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Head shape may be encoded in time-dependent rather than steady voltage patterns
statement: Because single-image voltage distributions showed no simple correspondence with the head shapes of octanol-treated G. dorotocephala, the authors consider it most likely that shape outcomes are encoded in time-dependent bioelectric activity rather than in steady voltage distributions, as in information encoding in the central nervous system.
quote: The most likely explanation however is that shape outcomes may not be encoded via steady (single-image) distributions but in time-dependent activity, as occurs during information encoding in the central nervous system.
scope: Planarian bioelectric patterns and head-shape outcomes

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Planarian morphology behaves as a homeostatic parameter maintained toward a target shape
statement: In planarians, morphology appears to be a homeostatic parameter that is repeatedly assessed and adjusted to maintain a 'target' morphology: after an incorrect head shape is produced during regeneration, the mismatch with the target triggers remodeling (between days 10 and 17 in octanol-treated G. dorotocephala), even after large-scale reorganization has ended.
quote: Morphology appears to be a homeostatic parameter, one that is consistently assessed and adjusted in order to maintain some “target” morphology.
scope: Regenerating and remodeling planarians (G. dorotocephala)

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Gap-junction-dependent instructive signals pass from somatic tissue to neoblasts
statement: The authors propose that significant instructive, gap-junction-dependent signaling passes from planarian somatic tissues to neoblasts or their progeny to guide new tissue generation and shaping during regeneration.
quote: In this model, we propose that significant instructive (GJ-dependent) signaling occurs from the somatic tissues to the neoblasts or their progeny, to guide the new tissue generation and shaping during regeneration.
scope: Regenerating planarian heads

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Somatic cells can be modeled as a slow neural-like network obeying brain-like dynamics
statement: The authors propose conceptualizing the link between gap junctional connectivity among planarian cells and discrete regenerative outcomes by viewing the cells as a neural-like network that processes developmental information more slowly but obeys the same statistical dynamics as the brain.
quote: Thus, we propose that one way to conceptualize the linkage between bioelectrical connectivity among worm cells (GJC) and discrete global behavioral outcomes achieved by regeneration is to view the worms’ cells as a neural-like network, processing developmental information more slowly but obeying the same statistical dynamics rules as are known to occur in the brain (Figure 9A).
scope: Planarian somatic cell networks during regeneration

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Planarian head shapes may be attractors of a gap-junction-coupled bioelectric network
statement: The authors hypothesize that distinct planarian head shapes may be attractors in the state space of the bioelectric network formed by body cells coupled by gap junctions, that these attractors correspond to regions of morphospace in the evolutionary sense, and that octanol knocks the network's stochastic dynamics into one of several nearby attractors normally belonging to other flatworm species.
quote: We hypothesize that distinct shape outcomes may be attractors in a state space describing distinct modes of the bioelectric network of planarian body cells connected by gap junctions (electrical synapses); in essence, these attractors correspond to regions of a morphospace as classically understood by evolutionary theory [151].
scope: Planarian body-wide bioelectric networks (G. dorotocephala and related species)

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Regeneration as descent to a free-energy attractor; induced shapes as local minima
statement: On the authors' proposed view, discrete planarian head patterns are the lowest free-energy outcomes of bioelectric network dynamics; amputation raises free energy and regeneration is a return to a low-energy attractor, octanol shifts the system to another attractor, and the induced other-species shapes are only local minima since worms return to the global minimum of G. dorotocephala morphology after about 3–4 weeks.
quote: On this view (Figure 9), the discrete head patterns are outcomes of bioelectric network dynamics with the lowest free-energy; cutting the network raises the free energy by deviating the system from its optimal morphology (damage), and initiates the regenerative process—a journey back down to a low-energy attractor.
scope: Planarian regeneration conceived as dynamics of a bioelectric network

work: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms
label: Planarian evolutionary distance may reflect ease of shifting a shared patterning network
statement: The authors suggest that a core network of gene-regulatory elements and gap-junction-mediated signals may be shared among many planarians, with species differences tweaking its dynamics, so that evolutionary distance between planarian species may reflect how easily this network can be shifted into its different outcome states, as during gap junction inhibition.
quote: The evolutionary distance among the planarian types may thus be expected to reflect the ease of shifting this network into its different potential outcome states (as occurs during GJC inhibition).
scope: Planarian species (Girardia, Dugesia, Schmidtea, Polycelis/Phagocata)

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: Resting potential of distant cells controls oncogene-dependent tumorigenesis
statement: The resting membrane potentials of cells located at a distance from oncogene-expressing cells are critical for whether those oncogene-expressing cells go on to form tumors in vivo, as shown in Xenopus laevis tadpoles injected with human oncogenes.
quote: Extending prior work focused on the bioelectric state of cancer cells themselves, we show for the first time that the resting potentials of distant cells are critical for oncogene-dependent tumorigenesis.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos/tadpoles injected with human or Xenopus oncogene mRNAs (Xrel3, Gli1, KRASG12D)

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: Oncogene-induced tumor-like structures in Xenopus share hallmarks of human tumors
statement: Tumor-like structures induced in Xenopus laevis tadpoles by human oncogenes such as mutant KRAS display overproliferation, increased nuclear size, hypoxia, intracellular acidity and leukocyte attraction, hallmarks shared with classic human tumors.
quote: In the Xenopus laevis tadpole model, we used human oncogenes such as mutant KRAS to drive formation of tumor-like structures that exhibited overproliferation, increased nuclear size, hypoxia, acidity, and leukocyte attraction.
scope: Induced tumor-like structures (ITLS) in Xenopus laevis embryos injected with Xrel3, Gli1 or KRASG12D mRNA

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: Remote Kv1.5 hyperpolarization suppresses tumor-like structures from two oncogenes
statement: In Xenopus laevis embryos, misexpressing the hyperpolarizing potassium channel Kv1.5 in a blastomere distant from the oncogene-injected blastomere reduces the incidence of induced tumor-like structures by about 35% for Xrel3 and about 29% for Gli1, indicating the suppression is not specific to one oncogene.
quote: Kv1.5-induced long-distance hyperpolarization was also able to significantly suppress Xrel3 and Gli1 ITLS formation by 34.9% (N=225; t-test, P<0.05) and 29.4% (N=292; t-test, P<0.05), respectively (Fig. 2C), suggesting the effect is not specific for just one type of oncogene.
scope: 16-cell-stage Xenopus laevis embryos co-injected with Xrel3 or Gli1 and Kv1.5 mRNA in separate blastomeres, scored at stage 34

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: High-chloride hyperpolarization suppresses KRAS tumors, so the effect is ion-independent
statement: Raising extracellular chloride, which hyperpolarizes cells through native chloride channels, decreases the incidence of KRASG12D-induced tumor-like structures in Xenopus laevis embryos by about 38%, showing that tumor suppression depends on the change in membrane voltage rather than on the Kv1.5 channel or on potassium specifically.
quote: Treatment with high chloride (whose uptake by native Cl− channels hyperpolarizes cells) resulted in a 37.5% decrease (N=349; t-test P<0.05) in KRASG12D ITLS, demonstrating that the suppressive effect is not specific for Kv1.5 nor for potassium, as mediators of the crucial Vmem change (Fig. 2C).
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos injected with KRASG12D mRNA and raised in elevated (70 mM) chloride medium

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: Native CLIC1 mediates chloride-based long-range tumor suppression
statement: The endogenous chloride intracellular channel 1 (CLIC1) is required for chloride-driven, long-range suppression of oncogene-induced tumor-like structures in Xenopus laevis, because non-local overexpression of wildtype CLIC1 increases suppression while a dominant-negative CLIC1C24S mutant blocks suppression even under high extracellular chloride.
quote: In contrast, overexpression of the mutant CLIC1 (N=336) effectively blocked ITLS suppression despite the presence of high Cl− (Fig 4C). Together, these data suggest a role for native CLIC1 in mediating hyperpolarization-induced long-range ITLS suppression.
scope: 16-cell-stage Xenopus laevis embryos injected with KRASG12D plus wildtype or dominant-negative CLIC1 in a separate blastomere, raised in 70 mM chloride

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: HDAC1 activity transduces remote voltage change into tumor suppression
statement: Histone deacetylase 1 activity is the main transduction step by which hyperpolarization of distant cells suppresses tumorigenesis in Xenopus laevis, since expressing a dominant-negative HDAC1 at a site remote from KRASG12D-expressing cells raises the incidence of induced tumor-like structures by about 36%.
quote: introducing DN-HDAC1 non-locally to the site of KRASG12D increased ITLS formation incidence by 35.6% (χ2, P<0.05) (Fig. 5C), suggesting a role for histone deacetylase 1 activity controlling cell behavior at a distance.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos injected with KRASG12D and dominant-negative HDAC1 mRNA in separate blastomeres under hyperpolarizing high-chloride conditions

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: Antibiotics against gram-positive bacteria increase tumor incidence
statement: Treating Xenopus laevis embryos with antibiotics that target gram-positive bacteria — novobiocin alone, or a cocktail of gentamicin, metronidazole, vancomycin and clindamycin — significantly increases the incidence of oncogene-induced tumor-like structures, implying that native butyrate-producing bacteria normally restrain tumorigenesis.
quote: Finally, a cocktail of antibiotics (gentamicin, metrodinazole, vancomycin hydrochloride, and clindamycin hydrochloride, all at 20 μM concentration) targeting gram-positive bacteria resulted in a significant increase in ITLS incidence by 26.2% (χ2, P<0.05) (Fig. 6).
scope: Oncogene-injected Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to antibiotics in the rearing medium

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: Vmem controls tumorigenesis via bacterially derived butyrate acting on HDAC1
statement: Control of oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis by resting membrane potential in Xenopus laevis is mediated by histone deacetylase 1, whose inhibition depends on butyrate produced by native gram-positive bacteria.
quote: Together, these data suggest that the control of tumorigenesis by Vmem is mediated by HDAC1, via butyrate derived from gram-positive bacteria.
scope: Oncogene-injected Xenopus laevis embryos with hyperpolarizing treatments, antibiotic treatments and dominant-negative HDAC1

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: Tumors may themselves emit bioelectric information detectable at a distance
statement: The authors speculate that long-range bioelectric connections in tumorigenesis are bidirectional, so that in addition to remote tissue voltage influencing tumor growth, tumors may emit bioelectric information that could be detected at a distance.
quote: It is tempting to speculate that the long-range connections are bi-directional: not only does remote electrical state of tissue matter for tumor growth, but perhaps tumors also emit bioelectrical information that could be detectable at a distance.
scope: Tumor–host bioelectric signaling, to be tested with molecular reagents in Xenopus and other models

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: Resting potential as a systems-level causal factor rather than specific channels
statement: Because tumor suppression was obtained with either chloride- or potassium-based hyperpolarization, the authors argue that a systems-level physiological property — resting membrane potential — rather than any specific ion channel acting as an oncogene or tumor suppressor, can be a powerful causal factor regulating tumorigenesis.
quote: Thus, in complement to the gene-focused idea of specific ion channels being intrinsic oncogenes or tumor suppressors [44, 48, 145], we suggest that a systems-level physiological property – resting potential – can be a powerful causal factor in regulating these processes.
scope: Bioelectric control of tumorigenesis generally, argued from Xenopus laevis oncogene experiments

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: Hyperpolarization skews butyrate-producing bacteria toward depolarized oncogene cells
statement: In the model the authors propose, hyperpolarized cells present a positively charged outer surface that reduces bacterial viability, so butyrate-producing bacteria are distributed away from hyperpolarized cells and toward the depolarized oncogene-expressing cells, where the resulting butyrate inhibits HDAC and promotes histone hyperacetylation and cell cycle arrest.
quote: As a result, distribution of butyrate producing-bacteria is skewed away from hyperpolarized cells in favor of oncogene-expressing cells, which are known to be depolarized pre-neoplastic transformation [43].
scope: Proposed model for Xenopus laevis embryos bearing oncogene-induced tumor-like structures and hyperpolarized remote tissue

work: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range
label: If conserved in mammals, Vmem modulation offers cancer detection and treatment routes
statement: The authors predict that if the role of remote endogenous bioelectric states in tumorigenesis is conserved in mammalian cancer models, modulation of resting membrane potential — potentially with ion channel drugs already approved for human use — would provide new cancer detection and treatment modalities.
quote: Future work must also examine the roles of remote endogenous bioelectric states in mammalian cancer models; if conserved, these data suggest a number of detection and treatment modalities focused on Vmem modulation.
scope: Mammalian cancer models and, by extension, human cancer therapy

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: Embryonic nicotine exposure causes major brain malformations in Xenopus
statement: Exposing Xenopus laevis embryos to nicotine (0.1 mg/mL, stages 10–35) causes major brain morphology defects (absent nostrils, forebrain or midbrain, misformed hindbrain) in about 55% of tadpoles at stage 45, compared with about 6% of controls.
quote: Nicotine exposure caused a significantly high incidence of major brain morphology defects (~55%) in comparison to controls (~6%).
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to 0.1 mg/mL nicotine from stage 10 to 35, scored at stage 45

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: BETSE model: leak and Kir channels produce a hyperpolarized neural tube prepattern
statement: In a BETSE bioelectric model of the stage 15 Xenopus neurula, regional differences in K+ and Cl− leak permeability open Kir channels in the neural tube, producing a Vmem of about −50 mV there while the neural folds and ectoderm stay near −5 mV, matching observed embryonic Vmem patterns.
quote: This results in open Kir channels in the hyperpolarized neural tube region leading to a Vmem pattern of approximately −50 mV in the neural tube region, while the lateral neural folds and ectoderm remain at ~−5 mV (Fig. 3a, e).
scope: BETSE model of an anterior view of the stage 15 Xenopus neurula surface in 0.1× MMR

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: Nicotine depolarizes the neural plate prepattern by about 15 mV, as the model predicted
statement: In stage 15 Xenopus embryos, nicotine treatment significantly reduces the endogenous neural hyperpolarization signal (a depolarization of about 15 mV, measured by calibrated voltage-dye imaging), matching the BETSE model's prediction in direction and magnitude.
quote: Nicotine-treated embryos showed significant reduction in endogenous neural Vmem signal (depolarization by ~15 mV) in comparison to controls (Figs. 4a, b, e, f, and Supplementary Figure 1). This observation matches the BETSE model predictions of nicotine effect on Vmem both in direction (depolarization) and magnitude (~15 mV).
scope: Neural plate and flanking ectoderm of stage 15 Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to nicotine

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: Nicotine causes brain defects by disrupting the endogenous bioelectric prepattern
statement: The authors' BETSE model explains nicotine-induced brain defects in Xenopus as resulting from nicotine's disruption of the endogenous bioelectric prepattern (neural tube hyperpolarization) required for brain development.
quote: Our model explains why nicotine induces brain defects: it correctly predicts the disruptive effects of this teratogen on the endogenous bioelectric prepattern required for brain development.
scope: Xenopus laevis neurula and brain development under nicotine exposure

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: Normal brain patterning needs the Vmem difference between neural tube and lateral tissue
statement: In Xenopus brain development, it is the spatial contrast of Vmem that matters: depolarizing the neural tube region or hyperpolarizing the lateral regions both cause brain defects, because the precise differential bioelectric state induces the balance of proliferation, apoptosis and gene expression needed to build a normal brain.
quote: The spatial patterning is crucial, as both depolarization of the middle region, or hyperpolarization of the lateral regions, both cause brain defects—it is the precise differential bioelectric state that induces the required balance of proliferation, apoptosis, and gene expression to build a normal brain28,48.
scope: Neural tube and surrounding ectoderm of Xenopus neurula-stage embryos

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: HCN2 modelled as a voltage-controlled switch that amplifies small Vmem gradients
statement: In the BETSE model of the Xenopus neurula, HCN2 channels open at hyperpolarized membrane voltage and hyperpolarize further when open, so they act as a voltage-controlled switch that amplifies small existing Vmem gradients: sufficiently negative neural tube cells go very hyperpolarized while depolarized lateral regions are left unchanged.
quote: HCN2 channels are predicted to open at hyperpolarized Vmem, generating more hyperpolarization with opening, thereby serving as a Vmem-controlled switch of Vmem state, capable of amplifying small Vmem gradients, similar to IT effect (Fig. 3c, e, f).
scope: BETSE bioelectric model of an anterior stage-15 Xenopus neurula

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: BETSE model predicts HCN2 maintains the neural tube Vmem pattern despite nicotine
statement: The BETSE model predicts that uniformly expressed HCN2 channels, which open at hyperpolarized Vmem and so amplify small Vmem gradients, open preferentially in the Xenopus neural tube and maintain its hyperpolarized Vmem pattern even in nicotine-exposed model embryos.
quote: Importantly, our model predicts that HCN2 expression leads to maintenance of neural tube Vmem pattern even in nicotine-exposed model embryos, similar to the action of IT (Fig. 3c vs. d, e, f).
scope: BETSE model of the Xenopus neurula with HCN2 channels (mouse kinetics, Na+:K+ permeability ratio 0.2) and nicotine

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: Measured HCN2 hyperpolarization in vivo was about half the model's prediction
statement: Hcn2 mRNA injection hyperpolarized the neural Vmem signal of Xenopus embryos by about 15 mV relative to controls, whereas the BETSE model predicted about 30 mV.
quote: However, the extent of enhanced hyperpolarization predicted by BETSE model for IT and HCN2 was higher (~30 mV) than actually observed (~15 mV) (Figs. 3e and 4).
scope: Xenopus laevis neurula-stage embryos injected with Hcn2-WT mRNA

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: HCN2 expression restores the neural Vmem prepattern despite nicotine
statement: In nicotine-exposed Xenopus embryos, expression of HCN2 channels enhances the neural-tube-specific hyperpolarization and restores the endogenous Vmem prepattern that nicotine otherwise suppresses, as the BETSE model predicted.
quote: As predicted, nicotine exposure suppresses the neural brain-specific Vmem pattern, while HCN2 channel expression enhances the neural Vmem pattern and restores it even in presence of the otherwise teratogenic nicotine.
scope: Xenopus laevis neurula-stage embryos exposed to nicotine, with or without Hcn2-WT mRNA

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: HCN2 reduces even minor background brain defects in untreated embryos
statement: In untreated Xenopus embryos, Hcn2 mRNA injection reduced the incidence of minor deviations from ideal brain morphology from about 9% to about 1.5%, so HCN2 improved patterning beyond that of unperturbed controls.
quote: Thus, misexpression of HCN2 channels resulted in an improvement of developmental patterning even beyond that observed in control populations of unperturbed embryos raised under optimal conditions.
scope: Wild-type Xenopus laevis embryos injected with Hcn2-WT mRNA, scored at stage 45

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: HCN2 fully rescues nicotine-induced brain malformations to control levels
statement: Injection of Hcn2-WT mRNA into nicotine-exposed Xenopus embryos reduced the incidence of major brain morphology defects from about 60% to about 6%, indistinguishable from untreated controls (about 7%).
quote: Remarkably, Hcn2-WT mRNA-injected embryos showed a complete rescue of brain morphology defects from nicotine exposure, to levels (~6%) indistinguishable from that of untreated control embryos (~7%) (Fig. 5f).
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to nicotine (0.1 mg/mL, stages 10–35), injected with Hcn2-WT mRNA

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: Dominant-negative HCN2 does not rescue nicotine brain defects
statement: Nicotine-exposed Xenopus embryos injected with a dominant-negative, non-conducting HCN2 mutant showed no rescue of brain morphology defects (about 70% defective), so the rescue depends on HCN2 channel conductance.
quote: In contrast, nicotine-exposed embryos injected with a mutant, dominant-negative form of HCN2 failed to show rescue of brain morphology defects (~70%) (Fig. 5f).
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to nicotine (0.1 mg/mL, stages 10–35), injected with Hcn2-DN (GYG→AAA pore mutant) mRNA

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: HCN2 restores wild-type brain shape in nicotine-exposed tadpoles
statement: Geometric morphometrics of stage-45 tadpoles show that nicotine significantly changes brain shape relative to the head, while nicotine-exposed tadpoles injected with Hcn2-WT mRNA do not differ in shape from controls.
quote: Thus, nicotine significantly changes brain shape, but Hcn2-WT mRNA microinjections restore brain morphology to the wild-type state.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to nicotine (0.1 mg/mL, stages 10–35), with or without Hcn2-WT mRNA

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: HCN2 restores learning in nicotine-exposed tadpoles
statement: In an automated red-light avoidance assay, only about 12% of nicotine-exposed Xenopus tadpoles learned, versus 100% of controls, and about 85% of nicotine-exposed tadpoles injected with Hcn2-WT mRNA learned.
quote: However, nicotine-exposed embryos receiving Hcn2-WT mRNA showed significant improvement in learning ability (85%, n = 20) in comparison to nicotine-exposed tadpoles (Fig. 7b, c, ANOVA, p < 0.001).
scope: Morphologically normal Xenopus laevis tadpoles exposed to nicotine as embryos, with or without Hcn2-WT mRNA

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: HCN2 rescue corrects otx2 and xbf1 expression after nicotine
statement: Nicotine reduces or mispatterns expression of the forebrain/midbrain transcription factors otx2 and xbf1 in Xenopus embryos, and Hcn2-WT mRNA injection restores their normal expression, linking HCN2-mediated repair to the known genetic cascade of brain patterning.
quote: Thus, HCN2 channel rescue of nicotine-induced defects includes correction of otx2 and xbf1, connecting HCN2-mediated repair of brain to the known molecular-genetic cascade of brain patterning factors.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos at stage 25, nicotine-exposed from stage 10, with or without Hcn2-WT mRNA

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: Native HCN2 activity is not required for normal brain patterning
statement: Because a dominant-negative HCN2 construct does not disrupt brain patterning, native HCN2 channel activity is not required for normal Xenopus brain patterning, ruling out the possibility that nicotine causes defects by directly blocking endogenous HCN2.
quote: However, our experiments with dominant-negative HCN2 channel shows that native HCN2 channel activity is not required for proper brain patterning (Supplementary Figure 4), thus negating this possibility.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos injected with Hcn2-DN mRNA

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: HCN2's restorative action may extend to many teratogens and lesions
statement: The authors suggest that HCN2's ability to improve brain morphology even in control embryos points to a general mechanism, reinforcing endogenous bioelectric signals needed for correct brain morphology, that could repair defects caused by a wide range of teratogens or physiological and genetic lesions, not only nicotine.
quote: These observations suggest that the restorative action of HCN2 is not limited to nicotine-induced brain morphology defects, but could reveal a more general mechanism of action, reinforcing the endogenous bioelectrical signals required for correct developmental brain morphology that might be partially destabilized by a wide range of exogenous teratogens or endogenous physiological/genetic lesions.
scope: Developing vertebrate brain (shown in Xenopus) exposed to teratogens or carrying physiological or genetic lesions

work: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns
label: Reagents that sharpen bioelectric compartment borders reinforce normal patterning
statement: The BETSE model predicts that reagents that sharpen the borders between bioelectric compartments, such as the context-sensitive HCN2 channel, will reinforce normal developmental patterning, a prediction confirmed for HCN2 in vivo.
quote: Most importantly, it predicts that reagents that sharpen borders between bioelectric compartments will reinforce normal patterning, thus identifying a context-sensitive HCN2 ion channel as an intervention tool.
scope: Embryonic brain patterning in Xenopus; proposed more generally for bioelectrically patterned tissues

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: A Self is bounded by a cognitive light cone of events it can measure and affect
statement: Any Self (agent) is demarcated by a computational surface, the spatio-temporal boundary of the events it can measure, model and try to affect; this surface is a cognitive "light cone" that sets the scale and limits of its cognition and allows agents of very different material make-up to be compared.
quote: Any Self is demarcated by a computational surface – the spatio-temporal boundary of events that it can measure, model, and try to affect. This surface sets a functional boundary - a cognitive “light cone” which defines the scale and limits of its cognition.
scope: All agents: biological, artificial and exobiological

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Somatic cells kept their computational capacities and scaled them to anatomical goals
statement: Somatic cells did not lose the behavioural plasticity and computational capabilities of their unicellular ancestors when they became part of metazoan bodies; they scaled them to pursue larger goals, namely building and maintaining complex anatomies.
quote: somatic cells did not lose their behavioral plasticity and computational capabilities in becoming part of metazoan swarms (bodies): they scaled them to enable pursuit of larger goals consisting of creation and upkeep of massively complex anatomies (Pezzulo and Levin, 2015).
scope: Metazoan somatic cells compared with unicellular ancestors

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Cell collectives pursue organ-level target morphologies despite perturbation
statement: Regulative development and regeneration (e.g. scrambled tadpole faces that still become normal frog faces, tail grafts remodelling into limbs, kidney tubules of constant diameter despite enlarged cells) show that somatic cells pursue specific target morphologies despite perturbation, with set points that are large organ-level macrostates not defined at the single-cell level.
quote: They reveal the ability of somatic cells to not only pursue specific target morphologies despite perturbations and novel scenarios, but to pursue collective patterning outcomes that are truly enormous with respect to the scale of size and organization of single cells
scope: Regulative development and regeneration in vertebrates (Xenopus, salamanders, axolotls, newts)

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Cell domains make coordinated group decisions, even random ones
statement: Cells join into domains that make decisions as a single unit: when left-right asymmetry is randomized in early embryos, a whole domain picks L or R identity rather than individual cells choosing independently, and in frog melanoma-like conversion all melanocytes in a body convert or not together.
quote: Remarkably, however, this randomization is made on a group level – in each case, the entire domain randomly picks L or R identity, not exhibiting a speckled appearance where each cell adopts a stochastic outcome. The decision is random, but all of the cells in the domain are coordinated to make the same random decision (Levin et al., 2002).
scope: Left-right patterning in early vertebrate embryos; melanocyte conversion in Xenopus tadpoles

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Neural motor control may be an exaptation of bioelectric navigation of morphospace
statement: Neural control of body movement in three-dimensional space may be an evolutionary exaptation and speed-up of an older, slower role of bioelectric signalling: moving the body's configuration through anatomical morphospace during embryogenesis, repair and remodelling.
quote: Neural networks control the movement of a body in three-dimensional space; this scheme may be an evolutionary exaptation and speed-optimization of a more ancient, slower role of bioelectrical signaling: the movement of body configuration through anatomical morphospace during embryogenesis, repair, and remodeling (Sullivan et al., 2016; Mathews and Levin, 2018; Mclaughlin and Levin, 2018).
scope: Evolution of nervous systems from developmental bioelectric signalling in animals

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Brain cognition lies on a continuum with conserved pre-neural computation
statement: Given the deep evolutionary conservation of ion-channel and neurotransmitter mechanisms between developmental and behavioural processes, the cognitive capacities of advanced brains are likely on a continuum with, and evolved from, much simpler computational processes conserved at both the functional and molecular levels.
quote: Thus, it is likely that the cognitive capacities of advanced brains lie on a continuum with, and evolve from, much simpler computational processes that are widely conserved at both the functional and mechanism (molecular) levels.
scope: Nervous systems and their pre-neural cellular precursors across the tree of life

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Disrupting or restoring cell communication should trigger or suppress cancer
statement: The shrinking-Self view of cancer predicts that interfering with physiological communication among cells should be able to trigger cancer and restoring it should suppress cancer, and that the relevant parameter (communication) is spread over considerable distance rather than confined to single cells as genomic damage is.
quote: This view predicts that interference with (or restoration of) physiological communication among cells should be able to trigger (or suppress) cancer and that the relevant parameter (communication) is spread out over considerable distance and not confined to single cells (e.g., genomic damage).
scope: Metazoan tissues; tested so far in amphibian models

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Depolarization induces and hyperpolarization prevents tumour-like changes in tadpoles
statement: In tadpoles, depolarizing a specific cell population is sufficient to cause metastatic-like transformation of normal melanocytes in genetically normal animals, while optogenetic or constitutive hyperpolarization prevents human oncogenes from inducing tumours.
quote: metastatic transformation of normal melanocytes can be achieved in genetically normal tadpoles simply by depolarizing a specific cell population (Lobikin et al., 2012), while, conversely, human oncogenes which normally induce tumors can be prevented from doing so simply by optogenetic or constitutive hyperpolarization (Chernet and Levin, 2013b, 2014; Chernet et al., 2015, 2016).
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles; melanocytes and human-oncogene-induced tumours

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Cancer cells are no more selfish than normal cells; their self is smaller
statement: Cells in a metazoan body are not less selfish than unicellular organisms or cancer cells; all are equally selfish, but the self that normal somatic cells defend is larger in space, time and complexity, its boundary being set by how far information passes between subunits.
quote: They are equally selfish, working only for the benefit of themselves, but the relevant self that they defend is bigger in terms of space, time, and complexity. As will be argued below, what defines this Self is the boundary of information being able to pass between the subunits.
scope: Somatic metazoan cells, cancer cells and unicellular organisms

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Most biological systems consist of multiple nested selves
statement: Under Scale-Free Cognition, most biological systems consist of multiple, nested selves rather than one, each inner agent maintaining its own Self only to the extent that it restricts information flow from its neighbours.
quote: It is an essential aspect of Scale-Free Cognition that most biological systems consist of multiple, nested selves [not one, as implied by Integrated Information Theory (Tononi, 2008)].
scope: Multilevel biological systems (molecular networks, cells, tissues, organs, organisms, swarms)

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: An Individual is defined by the scale and types of goals it can pursue
statement: The scale and types of goals (in the cybernetic sense of feedback toward a specific state) that a system can pursue define the boundaries and content of that system as an agent or Individual; the coherent Self is the set of parts that operate together toward specific goal states.
quote: I propose a definition of an Individual based on its information-processing structure (Barandiaran et al., 2009): the scale and types of goals that a system can pursue defines (determines) the boundaries and content of the putative “agent.”
scope: Biological individuals at any level of organization, plus artificial and exobiological agents

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Cognitive light cones have expanded over evolutionary time
statement: The volume of possible cognitive light cones (spatio-temporal boundaries of agents' goals) has presumably kept expanding over evolutionary time, through innovations in body structure that drastically enlarge the cognitive boundary, although some lineages contract it permanently or in particular life stages.
quote: Presumably, the volume of possible cognitive light cones keeps expanding with evolutionary time (although some lineages can contract it, permanently or during specific ontogenetic life stages). Over evolutionary scales, there have been “inflationary leaps” – innovations in body structure which drastically increase the cognitive boundary of viable selves.
scope: Evolution of agents across the tree of life

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Memory and learning are the origin of developmental modularity
statement: Memory can be the beginning of modularity because learning compresses complex states into simple triggers; in somatic control networks this appears as developmental modules in which a single simple driver (e.g. a bioelectric state) initiates a complex morphogenetic cascade such as building an eye or hand.
quote: Importantly, memory can serve as the beginning of modularity because learning essentially groups diverse stimuli into compressed representations: complex states of affairs become remembered as compact biophysical engrams – this is the essence of the kind of modularity when a simple biophysical event kicks off the formation of a complex morphogenetic cascade such as building a “hand” in embryogenesis.
scope: Developmental control networks in animals

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Animal senses use the same ion channel mechanisms found in bacteria
statement: The senses of complex animals (touch, taste, temperature, hearing, etc.) are mediated by the same ion channel mechanisms that bacteria already used to sense their world.
quote: Complex animals’ sense of touch, taste, temperature, hearing, etc. are mediated by the exact same ion channel mechanisms that were already discovered by bacteria and used to make sense of their world (Tasneem et al., 2005; Blackwell, 2006; Liebeskind et al., 2012; Nilius and Honore, 2012).
scope: Sensory ion channels in animals and their bacterial homologues
